plugins/llm/model_catalog.py:R8:_module_: os.environ.setdefault("LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP", "True") is a conditional WRITE of a process environment default, not a read of a key someone forgot to set, so R8's harm model (a missing key silently answered with a default) has no instance here: nothing downstream consumes a value this call invented. The absent case is the normal case and is the whole point of the line — litellm fetches its model-cost map from raw.githubusercontent.com at import time unless this variable is set, and elspeth-c67ba40e4a forbids a deployment silently egressing to a third party it never configured, so this module (ELSPETH's single point of truth for litellm access, imported before any lazy `import litellm` in the repo) pins the bundled map. The present case is equally deliberate: an operator who sets the variable themselves keeps their value and re-enables the remote fetch. Both branches are pinned by subprocess tests that a plain assignment would break — test_module_import_forces_litellm_local_cost_map (clean env must end up "True") and test_operator_override_of_litellm_cost_map_is_preserved (an explicit "False" must survive import). Respelling this as `if "LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP" not in os.environ: os.environ[...] = "True"` is byte-for-byte identical semantics and makes no previously hidden case visible, so it would be lint cosmetics rather than a fix.
plugins/llm/model_catalog.py:R5:read_lit: isinstance(raw, list) shape-checks `litellm.model_list`, an attribute of a third-party module ELSPETH does not own and cannot nominally type — measured directly: litellm resolves module attributes through its own module-level __getattr__ (litellm/__init__.py:2223), so the value's type is whatever the installed litellm version decided to publish, not a contract ELSPETH declares. ADR-032 says parse what we do not own, and this is that parse: the guard runs immediately after the direct attribute read and before the value reaches the sorted/str comprehension that builds the catalog. What it protects is load-bearing: read_litellm_model_list is the single source of truth behind the bundled OpenRouter slice, which is the validate-time set the value-source compliance walker checks every configured LLM model against, and whose sha256 is persisted to the Landscape `runs` table as openrouter_catalog_sha256 for audit reconstruction. A version-drifted litellm publishing a non-list here would otherwise be iterated blindly and poison that set. It is not covered by @trust_boundary because the decorator requires a source_param naming a real parameter and this function takes none (it is the @lru_cache'd public reader); extracting a two-line `_parse(raw)` helper purely to host the decorator would be indirection that exists only for the lint.

isinstance(m, str) is the per-entry half of the same Tier-3 parse of `litellm.model_list` (see the sibling R5 on the list check above): each element is an identifier published by a third-party module through litellm's own module-level __getattr__, not a value ELSPETH constructed. The filter is what makes the function's declared return type tuple[str, ...] true rather than aspirational, and the strings it admits become catalog membership — the walker rejects any configured `model` outside that set at validate time, and the OpenRouter provider puts the survivors on the wire. Admitting a non-string here would either crash the sort or land a nonsense identifier in the validate-time catalog and the persisted openrouter_catalog_sha256. Same reason as the sibling for not using @trust_boundary: the enclosing function has no parameter for source_param to name, and a helper introduced only to carry the decorator would be lint indirection.
plugins/llm/model_catalog.py:R6:prime_op: The httpx.RequestError is not swallowed — it is bound as `exc`, its class is emitted on the structured log channel (_slog.warning "openrouter_catalog_prime_transport_error" with url, exc_class and the action taken), and its effect is carried structurally: _clear_live_openrouter_catalog() runs so a failed re-prime cannot leave a stale live snapshot alive behind a "falling back" warning, and the False return is consumed by the one caller, web/app.py::_boot_prime_openrouter_catalog, which logs openrouter_catalog_boot_prime_failed with the probe latency. The fallback also reaches the audit trail, not just the logs: read_openrouter_catalog_snapshot_id then reports source="bundled", which the run-create writer persists to the Landscape `runs` table (openrouter_catalog_source / openrouter_catalog_sha256), so an auditor can reconstruct that a bundled catalog — not the live one — blessed every decision made in that process. Nothing about this failure is silent on any channel. Raising instead is the wrong outcome and is the specific thing this function is designed against: the caller is the FastAPI boot lifespan, so a raise crashes the web server on a transient OpenRouter outage, and the module's documented two-tier design requires the CLI and offline validate paths to work with the bundled catalog. R6 fires only because the explicit outcome is spelled as the documented `bool` return, which the rule classifies as a default value.

Identical structure to the transport-error handler above, for the narrower failure of a 200 response whose body is not JSON (a CDN or outage page served with HTTP 200): the ValueError is bound as `exc` and reported on the structured log channel as "openrouter_catalog_prime_decode_error" with url, exc_class and action; _clear_live_openrouter_catalog() prevents a stale live snapshot surviving a failed re-prime; the False return is consumed and re-logged by web/app.py::_boot_prime_openrouter_catalog; and the resulting bundled fallback is recorded in the Landscape `runs` table via openrouter_catalog_source so the audit trail names which catalog was in force. The catch is deliberately narrow — response.json() is the only statement inside the try — so it cannot mask an unrelated error, and it must not raise: the caller is the boot lifespan and this function's contract is that a malformed upstream body degrades to the bundled catalog rather than taking the web server down. R6 fires only because that explicit outcome is a documented bool.
